title: Lipo-C Fat Blaster (LC526)
summary: Lipo-C Fat Blaster (product code LC526) is a high-potency lipotropic injection built around a large carnitine dose, a full MIC base, and cellular-energy cofactors, aimed at maximizing fat-metabolism support without stimulants. It is a vitamin and amino acid blend rather than a peptide, delivered as a fixed direct dose with no titration. Each milliliter contains L-Carnitine 300mg, Methionine 25mg, Inositol 50mg, Choline 50mg, B12 (Methylcobalamin) 1mg, B6 (Pyridoxine) 50mg, and NADH 50mg. The high carnitine dose drives fatty-acid transport into the mitochondria, the MIC trio (methionine, inositol, choline) provides classic lipotropic fat-mobilization support, B6 and B12 support amino acid and energy metabolism, and NADH supplies a cellular energy cofactor that supports mitochondrial ATP production.
keyPoint: Lipo-C Fat Blaster (product code LC526) is a high-potency lipotropic injection built around a large carnitine dose, a full MIC base, and cellular-energy cofactors, aimed at maximizing fat-metabolism support without stimulants.

### compound | lipocfocuslc425/overview | What is Lipo-C Focus (LC425)?
kind: overview
title: Lipo-C Focus (LC425)
summary: Lipo-C Focus (product code LC425) is a stimulant-enhanced lipotropic injection designed to combine fat-metabolism support with a strong energy and mental-focus component. It is a vitamin and amino blend with added stimulant and cellular-energy ingredients, given as a fixed direct dose rather than a titrated peptide. Each milliliter contains ATP 50mg, Eria Jarensis 50mg, L-Carnitine 200mg, a MIC blend (Methionine 25mg, Inositol 50mg, Choline 50mg), Lidocaine 0.1 percent, and Benzyl Alcohol 2 percent. The high-dose carnitine and MIC base provide lipotropic fat-mobilization support, ATP supplies cellular energy substrate, Eria Jarensis is a stimulant that supports mood, drive, and focus, the lidocaine reduces injection discomfort, and benzyl alcohol acts as a preservative.

### compound | lipoclc120/overview | What is Lipo-C (LC120)?
kind: overview
title: Lipo-C (LC120)
summary: Lipo-C (product code LC120) is a lipotropic injectable blend built around the classic MIC-style fat-metabolism and methylation support stack. It is a vitamin and amino acid compound rather than a peptide, which means it does not act on a specific hormone receptor and does not require a titration or escalation schedule. Each milliliter of the blend contains Methionine 15mg, Choline Chloride 50mg, Carnitine 50mg, and Dexpanthenol (provitamin B5) 5mg. Methionine is a sulfur-containing essential amino acid that donates methyl groups and supports the liver in processing and exporting fat rather than storing it. Choline works alongside methionine to support hepatic fat transport and helps prevent fat from accumulating in the liver. L-Carnitine transports long-chain fatty acids into the mitochondria so they can be oxidized for energy, and Dexpanthenol supports the coenzyme-A pathway that fatty-acid metabolism depends on.
keyPoint: Lipo-C (product code LC120) is a lipotropic injectable blend built around the classic MIC-style fat-metabolism and methylation support stack.
understood: resolved
method: canonical
confidence: high
matchedText: Lipo-C (LC120)
  connectedTo: Lipo-C (LC120)
section: Why it is researched
  -: Lipo-C (product code LC120) is a lipotropic injectable blend built around the classic MIC-style fat-metabolism and methylation support stack.
section: How it works in the research
  -: Lipo-C (product code LC120) is a lipotropic injectable blend built around the classic MIC-style fat-metabolism and methylation support stack.
section: Evidence strength
  -: Peptide University Codex: Source summary; study design not clearly stated; population: Animal; Preclinical animal evidence. The source does not give a reliable study count.
section: Main limitations
  -: Known hypersensitivity to methionine, choline, L-carnitine, dexpanthenol, or any formulation excipient.
  -: Pregnancy or breastfeeding unless directed and supervised by a physician.
  -: Active liver or kidney disease unless medically supervised.
  followUp: Show the research evidence for Lipo-C (LC120)

### compound | lipoclc216/overview | What is Amino Lipotropic Complex (LC216)?
kind: overview
title: Amino Lipotropic Complex (LC216)
summary: The Amino Lipotropic Complex (product code LC216) is a broad-spectrum lipotropic and amino acid injection that expands on the basic MIC formula by adding performance and recovery aminos plus a fuller B-vitamin panel. It is a vitamin and amino acid blend rather than a peptide, working through nutritional and metabolic support pathways, and it is administered as a fixed direct dose without titration. Each milliliter contains L-Carnitine 20mg, L-Arginine 20mg, Methionine 25mg, Inositol 50mg, Choline 50mg, B6 (Pyridoxine) 25mg, B5 (Dexpanthenol) 25mg, and B12 (Methylcobalamin) 1mg. Carnitine, methionine, inositol, and choline provide the lipotropic fat-mobilization action, arginine supports nitric oxide production and blood flow, and the B6, B5, and B12 panel supports amino acid metabolism, energy production, and red blood cell formation.
keyPoint: The Amino Lipotropic Complex (product code LC216) is a broad-spectrum lipotropic and amino acid injection that expands on the basic MIC formula by adding performance and recovery aminos plus a fuller B-vitamin panel.

### compound | lipominomixlmx/overview | What is Lipo Mino Mix (LMX)?
kind: overview
title: Lipo Mino Mix (LMX)
summary: Lipo Mino Mix (product code LMX) is a well-rounded lipotropic and B-vitamin injection that pairs the classic MIC methylation base with a fuller B-vitamin panel and a solid carnitine dose. It is a vitamin and amino blend rather than a peptide, working through nutritional and metabolic support, and given as a fixed direct dose with no titration. Each milliliter contains B6 2mg, Methionine 12.4mg, Inositol 25mg, Choline 25mg, B1 (Thiamine) 50mg, B2 (Riboflavin) 5mg, and Carnitine 125mg. The methionine, inositol, and choline provide the lipotropic fat-transport base, carnitine supports mitochondrial fatty-acid oxidation, and the B1, B2, and B6 panel supports carbohydrate and amino acid metabolism and cellular energy production. In practice, Lipo Mino Mix is used by people who want a balanced, moderate-strength fat-metabolism and energy injection with a stronger B-vitamin profile than a bare MIC shot.
keyPoint: Lipo Mino Mix (product code LMX) is a well-rounded lipotropic and B-vitamin injection that pairs the classic MIC methylation base with a fuller B-vitamin panel and a solid carnitine dose.

### compound | liraglutide/evidence | What research is listed for Liraglutide?
kind: evidence
title: Liraglutide: research listed by the sources
summary: High evidence; 58 human studies listed strong-human. In LEADER, liraglutide reduced the primary major cardiovascular-event composite versus placebo in the studied adults with type 2 diabetes at high cardiovascular risk. In SCALE, liraglutide 3.0 mg was studied for weight management in adults with overweight or obesity. These are product-, dose-, population-, and endpoint-specific findings, not a general consumer-use or class-wide efficacy claim.
keyPoint: High evidence; 58 human studies listed strong-human.

  *: Source rating: 5 out of 5
  *: PepCodex: High evidence; 58 human studies listed
  *: The Peptide Handbook: strong-human. In LEADER, liraglutide reduced the primary major cardiovascular-event composite versus placebo in the studied adults with type 2 diabetes at high cardiovascular risk. In SCALE, liraglutide 3.0 mg was studied for weight management in adults with overweight or obesity. These are product-, dose-, population-, and endpoint-specific findings, not a general consumer-use or class-wide efficacy claim.
  *: PeptideDosage.org: Gastrointestinal effects are the most common adverse events: in SCALE roughly 39% of liraglutide 3.0 mg recipients reported nausea, about 15% vomiting, with diarrhea, constipation, dyspepsia and decreased appetite also frequent. Most were mild-to-moderate, peaked during the 4-5 week titration, and improved over time [1][7].; Symptoms are minimized by the slow weekly +0.6 mg escalation; manufacturers advise delaying a dose increase by an extra week (or stepping back down) if a titration step is not tolerated, and maintaining hydration to offset fluid losses [7].; Liraglutide carries an FDA boxed warning for thyroid C-cell tumors based on rodent carcinogenicity studies; it is contraindicated in patients with a personal or family history of medullary thyroid carcinoma (MTC) or multiple endocrine neoplasia syndrome type 2 (MEN 2). A causal link in humans has not been established [7][8].; Acute pancreatitis, including fatal and non-fatal hemorrhagic or necrotizing cases, has been reported post-marketing.
  *: PeptideDeck: Significant weight loss (5-10% body weight in clinical trials) Improved glycemic control and HbA1c reduction Cardiovascular risk reduction in type 2 diabetes Reduced appetite and food cravings Improved beta-cell function preservation Decreased fasting and postprandial glucose Potential neuroprotective effects under investigation Reduction in systolic blood pressure Liraglutide has been evaluated in an extensive clinical trial program involving tens of thousands of participants. The key trials can be grouped into those focusing on diabetes (LEAD and LEADER programs), weight management (SCALE program), and emerging indications. The Liraglutide Effect and Action in Diabetes: Evaluation of Cardiovascular Outcome Results (LEADER) trial was a landmark study published in the New England Journal of Medicine in 2016. This randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial enrolled 9,340 patients with type 2 diabetes and high cardiovascular risk, following them for a median of 3.8 years.
  *: WikiPep: LEADER trial results: The landmark LEADER (Liraglutide Effect and Action in Diabetes: Evaluation of Cardiovascular Outcome Results) trial demonstrated a 13% reduction in major adverse cardiovascular events (MACE) including cardiovascular death, nonfatal myocardial infarction, and nonfatal stroke. Cardiovascular death reduction: 22% reduction in cardiovascular death specifically. Renal benefits: Secondary analyses suggested reductions in the development and progression of diabetic kidney disease. LEAD program (Liraglutide Effect and Action in Diabetes): Six phase III trials establishing efficacy in type 2 diabetes across multiple treatment combinations. SCALE program: Four phase III trials demonstrating efficacy for weight management in obese and overweight populations. LEADER trial: Landmark cardiovascular outcomes trial (n=9,340) demonstrating cardiovascular safety and superiority, with 13% reduction in MACE over 3.8 years median follow-up. LIRA-RENAL trial: Demonstrated safety and efficacy in patients with moderate renal impairment.

### compound | livagen/overview | What is Livagen?
kind: overview
title: Livagen
summary: A synthetic tripeptide (Lys-Glu-Asp) developed by Russian scientist Vladimir Khavinson, claimed to support liver function and modulate hepatic gene expression. Minimal Western validation exists; all research originates from Russian institutions with no controlled human clinical trials.
keyPoint: A synthetic tripeptide (Lys-Glu-Asp) developed by Russian scientist Vladimir Khavinson, claimed to support liver function and modulate hepatic gene expression.
understood: resolved
method: canonical
confidence: high
matchedText: Livagen
  connectedTo: Livagen
section: Why it is researched
  -: A synthetic tripeptide (Lys-Glu-Asp) developed by Russian scientist Vladimir Khavinson, claimed to support liver function and modulate hepatic gene expression.
section: How it works in the research
  -: Livagen targets liver function through gene expression modulation and related pathways: Hepatic Gene Modulation Claimed to interact with DNA in hepatocytes, modulating expression of genes involved in liver function and regeneration.
section: Evidence strength
  -: PeptideDosage.org: Observational or case-based human research; population: Animal; Limited observational human evidence. The source does not give a reliable study count.
section: Main limitations
  -: Livagen is a synthetic tetrapeptide (Lys-Glu-Asp-Ala, KEDA) developed by Vladimir Khavinson and colleagues as a tissue-specific bioregulator targeting hepatic tissue and immune function [1][2].

### compound | livagen/evidence | What research is listed for Livagen?
kind: evidence
title: Livagen: research listed by the sources
summary: Livagen is generally well tolerated in Russian observational use; reported adverse effects are infrequent and mild.; The most common reported effect is transient injection-site discomfort with subcutaneous administration.; Occasional mild gastrointestinal upset (nausea, loose stools) has been reported with oral capsule formulations, particularly at higher milligram doses.; No tolerance, dependence, or withdrawal phenomena have been reported, consistent with epigenetic rather than receptor-occupancy mechanism.; Hypersensitivity reactions are rare; allergic skin responses to peptide preparations should prompt discontinuation.; Theoretical immune-modulating effects have not produced clinically significant autoimmune phenomena in published observational use, but the possibility cannot be excluded in patients with active autoimmune disease.; Drug-drug interaction data are not available; theoretical interactions with hepatically metabolized drugs are unstudied.; Reproductive, pregnancy, and lactation safety data are absent; use during these periods is not recommended. DNA Binding : Fluorescence spectroscopy confirmed KEDA tetrapeptide binds to specific DNA sequences, with preferential binding to AT-rich regions in hepatocyte gene promoters Chromatin Effects : Electron microscopy showed Livagen treatment caused decondensation of heterochromatin blocks in hepatocyte nuclei - indicating reactivation of silenced genes Gene Expression : Microarray analysis showed modulation of 42 genes in hepatocytes, including upregulation of albumin, transferrin, and CYP enzymes Animal Models : Improved liver function markers (ALT, AST, albumin) in aging rat models after 10-day Livagen treatment 🧪 Vial Dex The World's Most Advanced Peptide Calculator 100% FREE 💧 Reconstitution Vial + BAC water mixing 📉 Dose & Units Syringe units to draw 🔀 Blend Multi-peptide vial ratios 📚 Stack Protocol Multi-vial dose planning 💨 Nasal Spray Spray bottle concentrations 50+ Peptides 7 Calculators 0 Signup Required Peptide: Livagen Open Free Calculator → [ 1 ] [ 2 ] [ 3 ] [ 4 ] ↑ 1.0 1.1 Khavinson VK, et al.

section: Evidence strength
  -: PepCodex: Source summary; study design not clearly stated; population: Not clearly stated; Evidence level is not fully described by the source. The source does not give a reliable study count.
  -: PeptideDosage.org: Observational or case-based human research; population: Animal; Limited observational human evidence. The source does not give a reliable study count.

section: Limitations
  -: The source does not clearly state the study population or design in PEARL's reviewed record.
  -: Livagen is a synthetic tetrapeptide (Lys-Glu-Asp-Ala, KEDA) developed by Vladimir Khavinson and colleagues as a tissue-specific bioregulator targeting hepatic tissue and immune function [1][2].
  -: The reviewed record is animal research and cannot establish human effectiveness or safety.
  -: 14 Important Note This content is intended for therapeutic educational purposes only and does not constitute medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment.
  -: Active hepatocellular carcinoma or hepatic malignancy - Livagen's chromatin-decondensing activity and hepatocyte gene program normalization in malignant hepatocytes has not been evaluated; the epigenetic mechanisms underlying cancer involve both hypermethylation silencing of tumor suppressors AND hypomethylation of
  -: Active viral hepatitis with significant liver fibrosis (Metavir F3-F4) - the combination of active viral hepatic injury and chromatin bioregulator activity in severely fibrotic liver has not been characterized.
  -: Decompensated cirrhosis - insufficient viable hepatocyte mass for meaningful hepatic bioregulator response; the coagulopathy and portal hypertension of decompensated cirrhosis create an unfavorable context.
  -: Active systemic DNA damaging chemotherapy - the chromatin decondensation mechanism of Livagen could theoretically interfere with chemotherapy mechanisms that depend on chromatin accessibility for DNA-intercalating drugs or topoisomerase inhibitors.
  -: Known hypersensitivity to Livagen (Lys-Glu-Asp-Ala tetrapeptide) or formulation excipients.
  -: Pregnancy - chromatin-level gene regulatory modulation during embryonic and fetal development - when epigenetic gene programming is at its most active and tightly regulated - has not been evaluated and carries theoretical risk.
  -: Concurrent HDAC inhibitor therapy (vorinostat, romidepsin, valproic acid at chromatin-modifying doses) - the chromatin-modifying mechanisms of Livagen and HDAC inhibitors act on the same epigenetic regulatory machinery and could produce additive or unpredictable chromatin state changes.
  -: Active hematological malignancy - the chromatin-level gene regulatory activity could have unpredictable effects on malignant hematopoietic cell epigenetic programs.
  *: Source rating: 1 out of 5, very limited evidence
  *: PeptideDosage.org: Livagen is generally well tolerated in Russian observational use; reported adverse effects are infrequent and mild.; The most common reported effect is transient injection-site discomfort with subcutaneous administration.; Occasional mild gastrointestinal upset (nausea, loose stools) has been reported with oral capsule formulations, particularly at higher milligram doses.; No tolerance, dependence, or withdrawal phenomena have been reported, consistent with epigenetic rather than receptor-occupancy mechanism.; Hypersensitivity reactions are rare; allergic skin responses to peptide preparations should prompt discontinuation.; Theoretical immune-modulating effects have not produced clinically significant autoimmune phenomena in published observational use, but the possibility cannot be excluded in patients with active autoimmune disease.; Drug-drug interaction data are not available; theoretical interactions with hepatically metabolized drugs are unstudied.; Reproductive, pregnancy, and lactation safety data are absent; use during these periods is not recommended.

### compound | lixisenatide/overview | What is Lixisenatide?
kind: overview
title: Lixisenatide
summary: Lixisenatide (development code AVE0010; brands Adlyxin in the US and Lyxumia in the EU) is a once-daily, short-acting glucagon-like peptide-1 (GLP-1) receptor agonist developed by Sanofi for type 2 diabetes. It is a 44-amino-acid synthetic peptide derived from exendin-4, the GLP-1 mimetic first isolated from the saliva of the Gila monster (Heloderma suspectum); deletion of one proline and addition of six C-terminal lysine residues makes it resistant to dipeptidyl peptidase-4 (DPP-4) and gives it roughly four-fold higher affinity for the GLP-1 receptor than native GLP-1 [2]. Mechanistically it enhances glucose-dependent insulin secretion, suppresses glucagon, and markedly slows gastric emptying, producing its strongest effect on post-prandial glucose. The established Lixisenatide dosage is a simple two-step titration: 10 mcg subcutaneously once daily for 14 days, then 20 mcg once daily as the maintenance dose, injected within one hour before the first meal [1].
keyPoint: Lixisenatide (development code AVE0010; brands Adlyxin in the US and Lyxumia in the EU) is a once-daily, short-acting glucagon-like peptide-1 (GLP-1) receptor agonist developed by Sanofi for type 2 diabetes.

  *: The official label includes gastrointestinal, pancreatitis, kidney, hypoglycaemia and hypersensitivity warnings. [source-listed source severity]
  *: Nausea (25%) - most common, typically transient and dose-dependent Vomiting (10%) Diarrhea (8%) Headache (9%) Dizziness (5%). [source-listed source severity]
  *: Pancreatitis : Rare; discontinue if suspected Hypoglycemia : Increased risk when combined with sulfonylureas or insulin Anaphylaxis/Angioedema : Rare allergic reactions reported Immunogenicity : Anti-lixisenatide antibodies develop in ~70% of patients, though most are low-titer and do not affect efficacy. [source-listed source severity]
  *: Personal or family history of medullary thyroid carcinoma Multiple Endocrine Neoplasia syndrome type 2 (MEN 2) Known hypersensitivity to lixisenatide. [source-listed source severity]

### compound | lixisenatide/evidence | What research is listed for Lixisenatide?
kind: evidence
title: Lixisenatide: research listed by the sources
summary: Gastrointestinal effects are the most common adverse events: nausea (dose-dependent, roughly 20-25% in type 2 diabetes trials and as high as 46% on the 20 mcg dose in the LIXIPARK Parkinson's trial), vomiting, and diarrhea. Most are mild-to-moderate and are minimized by the 14-day 10 mcg lead-in before the 20 mcg maintenance dose [1][3][5].; Hypoglycemia is uncommon with lixisenatide monotherapy because insulin release is glucose-dependent, but risk rises substantially when it is combined with a sulfonylurea or insulin; the label advises reducing the sulfonylurea or insulin dose [1].; Acute pancreatitis is a recognized class risk for GLP-1 receptor agonists. Patients with persistent severe abdominal pain should stop the drug and be evaluated, and it should not be restarted if pancreatitis is confirmed [1].; Because lixisenatide is an exendin-based peptide, it is relatively immunogenic: most patients develop anti-drug antibodies, and a minority with very high antibody titers may show an attenuated glucose-lowering response. The GetGoal-Mono randomized trial studied 361 adults. The larger ELIXA cardiovascular trial enrolled 6,068 patients after acute coronary syndrome and found cardiovascular non-inferiority to placebo.
keyPoint: Gastrointestinal effects are the most common adverse events: nausea (dose-dependent, roughly 20-25% in type 2 diabetes trials and as high as 46% on the 20 mcg dose in the LIXIPARK Parkinson's trial), vomiting, and diarrhea.
understood: resolved
method: canonical
confidence: high
matchedText: Lixisenatide
  connectedTo: Lixisenatide
section: What the research shows
  -: PeptideDosage.org: Lixisenatide (development code AVE0010; brands Adlyxin in the US and Lyxumia in the EU) is a once-daily, short-acting glucagon-like peptide-1 (GLP-1) receptor agonist developed by Sanofi for type 2 diabetes.
  -: PeptideDeck: A short-acting GLP-1 receptor agonist studied and labelled for type 2 diabetes treatment in adults.
  -: WikiPep: From Wikipep - The Peptide Encyclopedia Lixisenatide Chemical name Lixisenatide Molecular formula C₂₁₅H₃₄₇N₆₁O₆₅S Molecular weight 4858.5 g/mol CAS number 320367-13-3 Sequence HGEGTFTSDLSKQMEEEAVRLFIEWLKNGGPSSGAPPSKKKKKK-NH₂ Length 44 amino acids Source Synthetic (exendin-4 derivative) Half-life 2-3 hours Targets GLP-1...
  -: PeptideJournal: Lixisenatide represents a distinctive approach among glucagon-like peptide-1 (GLP-1) receptor agonists: a short-acting peptide designed for once-daily administration that exerts its primary effects during the period immediately following meals.
section: Evidence strength
  -: PeptideDosage.org: Human clinical research; population: Human; Human evidence with design limitations to check. The source does not give a reliable study count.
  -: PeptideDeck: Randomized or controlled human research; population: Human; Direct controlled human evidence. 3 human studies listed by the source
  -: WikiPep: Animal research; population: Animal; Preclinical animal evidence. The source does not give a reliable study count.
  -: PeptideJournal: Animal research; population: Animal; Preclinical animal evidence. The source does not give a reliable study count.
section: Limitations
  -: Lixisenatide (development code AVE0010; brands Adlyxin in the US and Lyxumia in the EU) is a once-daily, short-acting glucagon-like peptide-1 (GLP-1) receptor agonist developed by Sanofi for type 2 diabetes.
  -: Official use depends on clinical context and monitoring.
  -: The US product was discontinued commercially, which is not the same as withdrawal for a safety finding.
  -: The reviewed record is animal research and cannot establish human effectiveness or safety.
  *: Source rating: 4 out of 5
  *: PeptideDosage.org: Gastrointestinal effects are the most common adverse events: nausea (dose-dependent, roughly 20-25% in type 2 diabetes trials and as high as 46% on the 20 mcg dose in the LIXIPARK Parkinson's trial), vomiting, and diarrhea. Most are mild-to-moderate and are minimized by the 14-day 10 mcg lead-in before the 20 mcg maintenance dose [1][3][5].; Hypoglycemia is uncommon with lixisenatide monotherapy because insulin release is glucose-dependent, but risk rises substantially when it is combined with a sulfonylurea or insulin; the label advises reducing the sulfonylurea or insulin dose [1].; Acute pancreatitis is a recognized class risk for GLP-1 receptor agonists. Patients with persistent severe abdominal pain should stop the drug and be evaluated, and it should not be restarted if pancreatitis is confirmed [1].; Because lixisenatide is an exendin-based peptide, it is relatively immunogenic: most patients develop anti-drug antibodies, and a minority with very high antibody titers may show an attenuated glucose-lowering response.
  *: PeptideDeck: The GetGoal-Mono randomized trial studied 361 adults. The larger ELIXA cardiovascular trial enrolled 6,068 patients after acute coronary syndrome and found cardiovascular non-inferiority to placebo.

title: LL37

A 37-amino acid peptide with broad-spectrum antimicrobial activity and immunomodulatory functions. Extensive mechanistic research supports roles in innate immunity, wound healing, and host defense.

### compound | ll37/evidence | What research is listed for LL37?
kind: evidence
title: LL37: research listed by the sources
summary: Solid human data for topical use (wound healing, antimicrobial). SubQ injection protocols are not supported by published clinical trials.
keyPoint: Solid human data for topical use (wound healing, antimicrobial).
understood: resolved
method: canonical
confidence: high
matchedText: LL37
  connectedTo: LL37
section: What the research shows
  -: PepCodex: The only human cathelicidin antimicrobial peptide, discovered at Karolinska Institute in Sweden (1995).
  -: The Peptide Handbook: The only known human cathelicidin antimicrobial peptide, naturally produced by immune cells, skin, and mucosal surfaces as part of the innate immune defense.
  -: Halflife Labs: LL-37 (cathelicidin) is a 37-amino-acid endogenous cationic peptide with a plasma half-life of minutes due to rapid proteolytic degradation.
  -: Peptpedia: The only human cathelicidin - destroys bacterial membranes and cuts biofilm mass 50-80% where antibiotics fail.
  -: PeptideDosage.org: LL-37 is the active form of human cathelicidin antimicrobial peptide (encoded by the gene CAMP), a 37-amino-acid amphipathic α-helical peptide cleaved from the precursor hCAP-18 by proteinase 3 in neutrophils and other tissues.
section: Evidence strength
  -: PepCodex: Human clinical research; population: Human; Human evidence with design limitations to check. 8 human studies listed by the source
  -: The Peptide Handbook: Animal research; population: Animal; Preclinical animal evidence. The source does not give a reliable study count.
  -: Halflife Labs: Animal research; population: Animal; Preclinical animal evidence. The source does not give a reliable study count.
  -: Peptpedia: Source summary; study design not clearly stated; population: Not clearly stated; Evidence level is not fully described by the source. The source does not give a reliable study count.
  -: PeptideDosage.org: Randomized or controlled human research; population: Human; Direct controlled human evidence. The source does not give a reliable study count.
section: Limitations
  -: The reviewed record does not state a specific limitation. The linked paper still needs to be checked for design, size and bias.
  -: Pro-inflammatory at high concentrations; paradoxical immune activation; cancer studies show context-dependent pro/anti-tumor effects
  -: no published human pharmacokinetic study.
  -: No clinical antibiotic replacement application has been approved to date; LL-37-based therapeutics are in early development stages.
  -: no approved therapeutic application exists.
  -: not medical advice, and the compounds covered are research chemicals not approved for human use unless explicitly stated otherwise.
  -: LL-37 is the active form of human cathelicidin antimicrobial peptide (encoded by the gene CAMP), a 37-amino-acid amphipathic α-helical peptide cleaved from the precursor hCAP-18 by proteinase 3 in neutrophils and other tissues.
  *: Source rating: 3 out of 5
  *: PepCodex: Moderate evidence; 8 human studies listed
  *: The Peptide Handbook: preliminary. LL-37 is the only known human cathelicidin antimicrobial peptide and is generated from hCAP18. Native LL-37 contributes to innate-immunity biology and has antimicrobial, endotoxin, biofilm, wound-related, and cancer-context research applications. The current evidence package is primarily mechanistic and preclinical; native LL-37, modified analogues, delivery systems, and the mouse homologue CRAMP are not interchangeable evidence entities. Human efficacy and a standardized clinical protocol are not established here.
  *: Halflife Labs: In-vitro and animal studies only; no published human pharmacokinetic study
  *: PeptideDosage.org: Subcutaneous injection of synthetic LL-37 can cause significant injection-site reactions including erythema, burning, induration, urticaria, and prolonged itching, reflecting the peptide's mast cell-degranulating and chemotactic properties.; LL-37 directly degranulates mast cells, potentially producing pseudo-allergic reactions, flushing, headache, and rarely systemic anaphylactoid responses, particularly in atopic individuals; this risk is greater with bolus injection than topical use.; Theoretical risks of exogenous LL-37 administration include exacerbation of rosacea, psoriasis, atopic dermatitis, and other conditions in which elevated endogenous cathelicidin is implicated in disease pathogenesis.; LL-37 has been shown to promote autoimmunity in genetically predisposed individuals through complexes with self DNA and RNA that activate plasmacytoid dendritic cell TLR7 and TLR9, with implications for systemic lupus erythematosus and other interferonopathies.; Local tolerability of topical LL-37 in wound healing trials has been acceptable, with mild burning or stinging at application
  *: PeptideDeck: Broad-spectrum antimicrobial activity against bacteria, fungi, and viruses Wound healing acceleration through keratinocyte migration Biofilm disruption and prevention Immunomodulatory effects balancing inflammation Angiogenesis promotion for tissue repair Neutralization of bacterial endotoxins (LPS) Synergistic effects with conventional antibiotics Skin barrier function enhancement LL-37 research spans three decades, with particular acceleration in recent years as the antibiotic resistance crisis has intensified. The following summarizes key findings across major research areas: Research published in Clinical Infectious Diseases (2008) demonstrated LL-37's ability to prevent Pseudomonas aeruginosa biofilm formation at sub-MIC concentrations and to promote the dispersal of pre-formed biofilms. This is particularly significant given that biofilm-associated infections account for approximately 80% of all chronic bacterial infections. Animal studies have consistently shown accelerated wound healing with LL-37 application.
  *: LL-37, the Only Human Member of the Cathelicidin Family of Antimicrobial Peptides (Biochimica et Biophysica Acta 2006): Comprehensive structural and functional review of LL-37 as the sole human cathelicidin, covering its amphipathic helical structure, broad-spectrum antimicrobial mechanism, and roles in infection, inflammation, and immune modulation.

  *: Resolved: modelled administration routes. Use only the route stated in the original study or official product information. Do not convert an oral, intranasal, intramuscular or investigational product into a generic subcutaneous vial protocol. PeptideDosage.org applies a common reconstitution and syringe format even to products such as Ventfort that it identifies as oral. That format is not evidence that the modelled route was studied or is suitable. Confidence: high.

Keep only links whose NCBI record matches the stated research subject. NCBI identifies PMID 11157505 as a Hodgkin-disease cell-fusion paper, PMID 16640009 as a Freeman-Sheldon syndrome case report, and PMID 18677858 as a neonatal-mortality paper. kind: overview
title: Longevity Master Stack

matchedText: Longevity Master Stack

  *: Source-listed components: Epithalon, Thymalin, MOTS-c, SS-31.
  *: The approved terminology source gives a fixed component list. Product strengths and protocols can still vary.
  *: Terminology confidence: medium. Commercial source terminology only. The combination is not treated as a clinical regimen.
  *: Naming limitation: The name is not scientifically standardised.
  *: No source in the approved library establishes that the combination itself has the same evidence as its individual components.
  *: Epithalon: Source rating: 2 out of 5, limited evidence. Russian research base. Animal telomere and lifespan data solid.
  *: Thymalin: Source rating: 2 out of 5, limited evidence. Russian clinical data (St. Petersburg Institute of Biogerontology). Limited Western RCT data.
  *: MOTS-c: Source rating: 2 out of 5, limited evidence. No completed human RCTs. Animal data strong. Human pilot studies range 5-10mg 2-3x weekly. Conservative approach recommended given experimental status. NOTE: Dosing protocols vary widely - some sources suggest daily low-dose (1-2mg), others suggest 5mg 2-3x weekly. We default to the more conservative 2-3x weekly protocol.
  *: SS-31: Source rating: 3 out of 5. Clinical trials used 4mg and 40mg daily SubQ - but these were in SICK patients (heart failure, Barth syndrome). Healthy biohacker doses are far lower: 1-10 mg/day is the typical range. The 40mg TAZPOWER dose was for a rare genetic mitochondrial disease; it is not a biohacker target. Safety is well-established up to 40mg/day from trial data, but therapeutic need does not apply to healthy users. Doses shown above reflect biohacker practice, not clinical trial protocols.

  *: Thymalin: Source rating: 2 out of 5, limited evidence. Russian clinical data (St. Petersburg Institute of Biogerontology). Limited Western RCT data.
  *: MOTS-c: Source rating: 2 out of 5, limited evidence. No completed human RCTs. Animal data strong. Human pilot studies range 5-10mg 2-3x weekly. Conservative approach recommended given experimental status. NOTE: Dosing protocols vary widely - some sources suggest daily low-dose (1-2mg), others suggest 5mg 2-3x weekly. We default to the more conservative 2-3x weekly protocol.
  *: SS-31: Source rating: 3 out of 5. Clinical trials used 4mg and 40mg daily SubQ - but these were in SICK patients (heart failure, Barth syndrome). Healthy biohacker doses are far lower: 1-10 mg/day is the typical range. The 40mg TAZPOWER dose was for a rare genetic mitochondrial disease; it is not a biohacker target. Safety is well-established up to 40mg/day from trial data, but therapeutic need does not apply to healthy users. Doses shown above reflect biohacker practice, not clinical trial protocols.

summary: From Wikipep - The Peptide Encyclopedia Lutetium-177 Dotatate Chemical name ¹⁷⁷Lu-DOTA-Tyr³-Octreotate (Lutathera) Molecular formula C₆₅H₉₂¹⁷⁷LuN₁₄O₂₆S₂ Molecular weight ~1,622 Da (with ¹⁷⁷Lu chelated) CAS number 1257084-44-0 Sequence D-Phe-Cys-Tyr-D-Trp-Lys-Thr-Cys-Thr (DOTA-chelated) Length 8 amino acids (somatostatin analog) + DOTA chelator Source Synthetic radiopharmaceutical Half-life 6.65 days (¹⁷⁷Lu physical half-life) Targets Somatostatin receptor subtype 2 (SSTR2) Bioavailability Intravenous (100%) Legal status FDA-approved (2018, Lutathera); EMA-approved (2017) Lutetium-177 Dotatate (trade name Lutathera , also written as ¹⁷⁷Lu-DOTATATE ) is an FDA-approved peptide receptor radionuclide therapy (PRRT) for the treatment of somatostatin receptor-positive gastroenteropancreatic neuroendocrine tumors (GEP-NETs) . ### compound | macimorelin/overview | What is Macimorelin?
kind: overview
title: Macimorelin
summary: Macimorelin (brand names Macrilen and Ghryvelin) is an orally active ghrelin/growth hormone secretagogue receptor (GHS-R1a) agonist used as a diagnostic agent for adult growth hormone deficiency (AGHD). Derived from a downsized analog of the GH-releasing peptide examorelin, this small-molecule secretagogue mimics ghrelin at pituitary and hypothalamic receptors to provoke a sharp, measurable release of growth hormone, which clinicians use to separate patients with an intact GH axis from those with deficiency [1][5]. The established Macimorelin dosage is a single 0.5 mg/kg oral dose taken after at least an 8-hour fast, with venous blood sampled at 30, 45, 60 and 90 minutes; a peak stimulated GH below 2.8 ng/mL confirms AGHD on the FDA-approved label [1]. In validation and pivotal trials, oral macimorelin matched the diagnostic accuracy of the insulin tolerance test and of arginine+GHRH testing while being simpler and safer to administer [2][3].
keyPoint: Macimorelin (brand names Macrilen and Ghryvelin) is an orally active ghrelin/growth hormone secretagogue receptor (GHS-R1a) agonist used as a diagnostic agent for adult growth hormone deficiency (AGHD).

  *: PeptideDosage.org: The most common adverse reaction in clinical testing was dysgeusia (an altered or metallic taste), reported in about 4.5% of subjects; this is generally transient and self-limited [1].; Dizziness, headache, and fatigue each occurred in roughly 3.9% of subjects, and were mild to moderate and short-lived after the single dose [1][4].; Gastrointestinal and appetite-related effects were reported, including nausea (about 3.2%), hunger (about 3.2%), and diarrhea (about 1.9%), consistent with ghrelin-receptor activation [1].; QT prolongation is the key safety signal: macimorelin increases the corrected QT interval by approximately 11 msec, so concomitant use with drugs that prolong QT (for example antipsychotics, fluoroquinolone antibiotics, and Class IA/III antiarrhythmics) should be avoided to limit arrhythmia risk [1][4].; Drug interactions can compromise the test result: strong CYP3A4 inducers (rifampin, carbamazepine, phenytoin, St.

### compound | maritide/overview | What is MariTide?
kind: overview
title: MariTide
summary: A bispecific peptide-antibody conjugate combining GLP-1 receptor agonism with GIP receptor antagonism. Unique mechanism opposite to tirzepatide. The published Phase 2 trial (NCT05669599) showed up to ~16% weight loss at 52 weeks with once-monthly dosing. MARITIME Phase 3 program ongoing.
keyPoint: A bispecific peptide-antibody conjugate combining GLP-1 receptor agonism with GIP receptor antagonism.

### compound | maritide/evidence | What research is listed for MariTide?
kind: evidence
title: MariTide: research listed by the sources
summary: Moderate evidence; 12 human studies listed Gastrointestinal effects are the most common adverse events: nausea, vomiting, and constipation predominated in the Phase 1 and Phase 2 trials. They were mostly mild-to-moderate, transient, and concentrated around the first dose, and resolved relatively quickly [1][2][7].; Gradual dose escalation markedly lowers gastrointestinal toxicity: arms that ramped to the 420 mg target over several months had fewer and milder GI events than those starting at a high fixed dose, which is why the Phase 3 program uses a multi-week low-dose initiation [1][7][8].; Treatment discontinuation for adverse events was roughly 11% in the Phase 2 trial, with GI-related discontinuations under about 8% - higher than placebo but consistent with the incretin drug class [1][7].; As a GLP-1 receptor agonist, MariTide carries class-level cautions shared with semaglutide, liraglutide, and tirzepatide, including potential acute pancreatitis, gallbladder events (cholelithiasis/cholecystitis) with rapid weight loss, and increased hypoglycemia risk when combined with insulin or sulfonylureas; these require clinician

### compound | matrixyl/overview | What is Matrixyl?
kind: overview
title: Matrixyl
summary: Matrixyl (palmitoyl pentapeptide-4, Pal-KTTKS) is a cosmetic collagen-stimulating matrikine peptide developed by the French active-ingredient house Sederma and launched in 2000. It pairs the procollagen-I matrikine sequence KTTKS (lysine-threonine-threonine-lysine-serine), naturally released from the C-terminal propeptide of type I procollagen, with a 16-carbon palmitic-acid chain that lets the otherwise hydrophilic pentapeptide cross the stratum corneum. Once in the dermis, KTTKS acts as a feedback signal that prompts fibroblasts to upregulate type I and III collagen, fibronectin, and glycosaminoglycans, the rationale behind its anti-wrinkle positioning.
keyPoint: Matrixyl (palmitoyl pentapeptide-4, Pal-KTTKS) is a cosmetic collagen-stimulating matrikine peptide developed by the French active-ingredient house Sederma and launched in 2000.

### compound | matrixyl/evidence | What research is listed for Matrixyl?
kind: evidence
title: Matrixyl: research listed by the sources
summary: Topical use is generally very well tolerated; the most common adverse effects are limited to mild, transient erythema, stinging, or a sensation of tightness at the application site, often when layered with other actives such as retinoids, vitamin C, or exfoliating acids [3][7].; Allergic contact dermatitis to pal-KTTKS itself is uncommon, but reactions to other components of a finished cosmetic (preservatives, fragrances, emulsifiers, or penetration enhancers) can cause eczematous patches and should be evaluated by a dermatologist if persistent.; Because finished products are applied to the face, accidental ocular contact may cause transient eye irritation, watering, and burning; keep product away from the eye margin and rinse with water if it migrates onto the ocular surface.; Systemic side effects have not been reported and are not expected: in vitro permeation shows pal-KTTKS reaches the stratum corneum, epidermis, and upper dermis but does not cross full-thickness skin into the circulation, so there is negligible systemic exposure [4].; Pregnancy, lactation, and pediatric safety A 12-week double-blind split-face randomized study enrolled 93 women and compared moisturizer containing 3 ppm pal-KTTKS with moisturizer alone.

  *: Resolved: site-listed dose ranges. Published study protocols with species, route, population, frequency and duration take priority. Uncited commercial ranges remain labelled and secondary.   *: Resolved: modelled administration routes. Use only the route stated in the original study or official product information. Do not convert an oral, intranasal, intramuscular or investigational product into a generic subcutaneous vial protocol. PeptideDosage.org applies a common reconstitution and syringe format even to products such as Ventfort that it identifies as oral. That format is not evidence that the modelled route was studied or is suitable. Confidence: high.
  *: Resolved: mental-health citation identity. Exclude three unrelated PubMed identifiers copied under Semax, NAC and Selank claims. Keep only links whose NCBI record matches the stated research subject. NCBI identifies PMID 11157505 as a Hodgkin-disease cell-fusion paper, PMID 16640009 as a Freeman-Sheldon syndrome case report, and PMID 18677858 as a neonatal-mortality paper. None supports the peptide claim beside which it appeared. Confidence: high.

### compound | matrixylsynthe6/evidence | What research is listed for Matrixyl Synthe-6?
kind: evidence
title: Matrixyl Synthe-6: research listed by the sources
summary: Most anti-aging peptides do one thing: boost collagen production. Matrixyl Synthe'6 does six. This third-generation peptide from Sederma takes a broader approach to skin repair, stimulating not just collagen but five other structural proteins that fill wrinkles from the inside rather than simply Matrixyl Synthe'6 represents a more sophisticated approach to peptide-based anti-aging. By stimulating six major components of the extracellular matrix rather than focusing solely on collagen production, it addresses multiple aspects of skin aging simultaneously: firmness (collagen I and III), elasticity (collagen III), structural integrity (collagen IV, laminin-5, fibronectin), and volume (hyaluronic acid). The clinical evidence, while limited to relatively short-term studies, shows genuine wrinkle reduction-around 31% improvement on average after 8 weeks of consistent twice-daily use. This puts it in the same ballpark as other evidence-based anti-aging ingredients like retinoids and vitamin C, with the advantage of being significantly gentler and better tolerated.

The GLORY-1 trial showed 14.0% weight loss at 48 weeks with the 6mg dose. The DREAMS-3 head-to-head trial vs semaglutide for combined diabetes + obesity outcomes is ongoing, with results not yet published.

  *: PeptideDosage.org: Gastrointestinal events were the most common adverse events across the Phase 2 and Phase 3 trials, with nausea reported in 30-40% of participants on active doses, vomiting in 15-20%, diarrhea in 12-18% and decreased appetite (the desired effect) in 25-35%. Most events were mild-to-moderate and concentrated during titration [1][2].; Heart-rate elevation of 4-6 beats per minute on average was observed across active arms, consistent with class effect for dual GCGR/GLP-1R agonists and slightly higher than seen with pure GLP-1 monotherapy.; Injection-site reactions occurred in roughly 5-8% of participants, including erythema, induration and pruritus. Most were mild and resolved with site rotation.; A small transient increase in fasting glucose was observed in non-diabetic participants during early titration, reflecting the glucagon-receptor agonism component.

  *: PeptideJournal: The global obesity epidemic has driven an explosion of interest in peptide therapeutics that can deliver substantial, sustained weight loss. Mazdutide represents a meaningful advance in peptide-based metabolic therapeutics, distinguished by its dual GLP-1/glucagon receptor mechanism. By combining appetite suppression and enhanced insulin secretion (via GLP-1) with increased energy expenditure and improved hepatic fat metabolism (via glucagon), the peptide offers a differentiated approach to weight management and glycemic control. Clinical trial data are compelling. Weight loss of 14-18% with approved doses compares favorably to first-generation GLP-1 agonists and approaches the efficacy of the most potent available therapies. Head-to-head comparison against semaglutide showed superiority for both weight loss and glycemic control in patients with type 2 diabetes. The particularly striking reductions in liver fat-up to 80% in some cohorts-position mazdutide as a potential therapy for metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease.

section: What the research shows
  -: PepCodex: An FDA-approved synthetic analog of alpha-MSH that selectively activates MC1R to stimulate eumelanin production.
  -: Peptpedia: The only FDA-approved melanocortin implant (Scenesse, 2019) - approved for EPP, not cosmetic tanning.
  -: PeptideDosage.org: Melanotan I (afamelanotide; brand name Scenesse) is a synthetic 13-amino-acid analogue of alpha-melanocyte-stimulating hormone (α-MSH) and a selective melanocortin-1 receptor (MC1R) agonist in the cosmetic/tanning melanocortin class.
  -: PeptideDeck: Recommended
  -: PeptideDeck: Recommended

  -: Peptpedia: Source summary; study design not clearly stated; population: Not clearly stated; Evidence level is not fully described by the source. The source does not give a reliable study count.
  -: PeptideDosage.org: Human clinical research; population: Human; Human evidence with design limitations to check. The source does not give a reliable study count.
  -: PeptideDeck: Human clinical research; population: Human; Human evidence with design limitations to check. The source does not give a reliable study count.
  -: PeptideDeck: Human clinical research; population: Human; Human evidence with design limitations to check. The source does not give a reliable study count.
section: Limitations
  -: The reviewed record does not state a specific limitation. The linked paper still needs to be checked for design, size and bias.
  -: not cosmetic tanning.
  -: no detectable drug, and the free peptide's short plasma half-life directly motivated the controlled-release implant that became the FDA-approved product Scenesse.
  -: no detectable plasma levels (PMID 9113347).
  -: not moment-to-moment drug levels (PMID 28063031).
  -: not pharmaceutical afamelanotide and have no dosing standard.
  -: no serious adverse events were attributed to the drug, the evidence base behind the 2019 FDA approval.
  -: no serious adverse effects reported to date.
  -: no detectable plasma levels.
  -: Melanotan I (afamelanotide; brand name Scenesse) is a synthetic 13-amino-acid analogue of alpha-melanocyte-stimulating hormone (α-MSH) and a selective melanocortin-1 receptor (MC1R) agonist in the cosmetic/tanning melanocortin class.
  -: Research-grade MT-I lacks the quality controls of pharmaceutical Scenesse. Purity, sterility, and accurate concentration cannot be guaranteed, introducing risks beyond the compound's inherent pharmacology.
  *: Source rating: 3 out of 5
  *: PepCodex: Moderate evidence; 6 human studies listed
  *: PeptideDosage.org: Nausea is the most consistent effect, reported in roughly 19% of implant recipients (versus ~14% on placebo) and frequently in injectable-liquid users; flushing, fatigue, dizziness, headache and somnolence are also common [1][4].; Implant- or injection-site reactions (pain, swelling, discoloration) occurred in about 21% of treated patients versus ~10% with placebo in the approval trials [1][4].; Generalized skin darkening is expected and intended, but moles and other pigmented lesions also darken; this can obscure early melanoma and is why a full-body skin examination twice yearly is advised for treated patients [4].; Case reports describe new or rapidly changing naevi and melanoma diagnoses associated with melanotan use; a causal link is unproven, but the signal is taken seriously and is a key reason cosmetic use is discouraged [6][8].; Because the injectable cosmetic product is unlicensed and grey-market, vials may be contaminated, mislabeled or wrongly dosed; injection of non-sterile or impure material adds infection and unknown-impurity risks beyond the peptide itself [6][8].;
  *: PeptideDeck: Stimulates natural melanin production Provides photoprotection independent of UV exposure Approved treatment for EPP in Europe/Australia More selective than Melanotan II (fewer side effects) May protect against UV-induced DNA damage Does not require sun exposure to work Potential skin cancer prevention applications No effect on sexual function (unlike MT-II) Active research area with published studies Melanotan I research spans basic melanocortin biology, clinical trials for EPP, and exploratory studies in photoprotection and skin conditions. The pivotal studies leading to Scenesse approval demonstrated that EPP patients receiving afamelanotide implants could tolerate significantly more time in sunlight without experiencing phototoxic reactions. The trials showed: Increased melanin density in skin Extended time to onset of prodromal symptoms Improved quality of life measures Acceptable safety profile These trials established that pharmacological melanogenesis could provide meaningful clinical benefit.
  *: PeptideDeck: FDA-approved photoprotection for erythropoietic protoporphyria (EPP) Stimulates natural eumelanin production for UV-independent tanning High MC1R selectivity with minimal off-target melanocortin effects Demonstrated efficacy in reducing phototoxic reactions in clinical trials Potential repigmentation therapy for vitiligo when combined with NB-UVB Extended duration of action via subcutaneous implant delivery Investigational photoprotection for organ transplant recipients May reduce DNA damage from UV exposure through enhanced melanin shielding Afamelanotide has the most extensive clinical trial program of any melanocortin peptide, with data from multiple Phase II and Phase III studies across several dermatological conditions. Here is what the evidence demonstrates: Vitiligo research represents afamelanotide's most advanced pipeline indication beyond EPP. A landmark 2013 randomized controlled trial published in JAMA Dermatology (Grimes et al.) evaluated afamelanotide combined with narrowband UVB (NB-UVB) phototherapy versus NB-UVB alone in 55 patients with generalized vitiligo.
  *: PeptideDeck: View All sexual health comparisons
  *: Afamelanotide for Erythropoietic Protoporphyria (New England Journal of Medicine 2015): Langendonk et al. Phase 3 RCT demonstrating afamelanotide (Scenesse/Melanotan I) significantly increased pain-free sun exposure time and reduced phototoxic reactions in EPP patients - the pivotal trial supporting FDA approval for this MC1R agonist.

### compound | melanotan-ii/evidence | What research is listed for Melanotan II?

title: Melanotan II: research listed by the sources
summary: Melanotan II is not an approved medicine. Evidence includes very small early human studies of pigmentation and erectile response; these do not validate commercial-use protocols.
keyPoint: Melanotan II is not an approved medicine.
understood: resolved
method: canonical

  connectedTo: Melanotan II
section: What the research shows
  -: PepCodex: A non-selective melanocortin receptor agonist known for tanning effects.
  -: The Peptide Handbook: A synthetic analog of alpha-melanocyte-stimulating hormone studied for its simultaneous effects on skin pigmentation, sexual arousal pathways, and appetite.
  -: Peptpedia: Tans without UV by activating melanocortin receptors - non-selectively, hence the broad side-effect profile.
  -: PeptideDosage.org: Melanotan II is a synthetic cyclic heptapeptide analog of alpha-melanocyte-stimulating hormone (α-MSH) developed at the University of Arizona by Hadley, Hruby, Dorr and colleagues in the 1980s as a stable, broadly active melanocortin receptor agonist.
  -: PeptideDeck: Recommended
section: Evidence strength
  -: PepCodex: Human clinical research; population: Human; Human evidence with design limitations to check. 8 human studies listed by the source
  -: The Peptide Handbook: Randomized or controlled human research; population: Not clearly stated; Direct controlled human evidence. The source does not give a reliable study count.
  -: Peptpedia: Source summary; study design not clearly stated; population: Not clearly stated; Evidence level is not fully described by the source. The source does not give a reliable study count.
  -: PeptideDosage.org: Human clinical research; population: Human; Human evidence with design limitations to check. The source does not give a reliable study count.
  -: PeptideDeck: Source summary; study design not clearly stated; population: Not clearly stated; Evidence level is not fully described by the source. The source does not give a reliable study count.
section: Limitations
  -: The reviewed record does not state a specific limitation. The linked paper still needs to be checked for design, size and bias.
  -: Small human studies reported nausea and unplanned erections; long-term dermatologic and cardiovascular safety has not been established
  -: no approved clinical indication.
  -: No Human Half-Life on Record: No peer-reviewed study reports a human plasma half-life for melanotan II.
  -: not human measurement - the cyclic structure improves stability over linear α-MSH but does not produce a long-acting compound.
  -: not reported (PMID 8637402).
  -: no equivalent formulation work exists for melanotan II (PMID 28063031).
  -: not approved by the FDA, EMA, or any major regulatory agency for any clinical indication.
  -: not necessarily provide equivalent photoprotection.
  -: no human trials specifically studying appetite suppression with MT-II have been published-the nausea side effect may confound any appetite-suppression measurement (vomiting reduces caloric intake independently of true satiety signaling).
  -: Melanotan II is a synthetic cyclic heptapeptide analog of alpha-melanocyte-stimulating hormone (α-MSH) developed at the University of Arizona by Hadley, Hruby, Dorr and colleagues in the 1980s as a stable, broadly active melanocortin receptor agonist.
  -: The source does not clearly state the study population or design in PEARL's reviewed record.
  *: Source rating: 2 out of 5, limited evidence
  *: PepCodex: Moderate evidence; 8 human studies listed
  *: The Peptide Handbook: preliminary. A small double-blind crossover study in men with erectile dysfunction reported erections and frequent adverse effects after Melanotan II. These limited observations do not establish safety or efficacy for tanning, sexual performance, or any other clinical use.
  *: PeptideDosage.org: Nausea, occasionally accompanied by vomiting, is reported by 50-80% of Melanotan II users, typically within thirty to ninety minutes of injection, and reflects central MC4R activation in brainstem nuclei controlling emesis; gradual dose titration partially attenuates this effect.; Facial flushing, yawning, fatigue, and dose-dependent transient elevations in blood pressure and heart rate are common, reflecting melanocortin-mediated effects on the autonomic nervous system and cutaneous vasculature.; Spontaneous penile erections in men and increased sexual arousal in both sexes occur due to MC4R activation in central reward and erectile circuits and can be inconvenient, embarrassing, or in rare cases prolonged.; Dermatologically, Melanotan II can cause the appearance of new pigmented melanocytic nevi, darkening and enlargement of pre-existing nevi, and irregularity of pigmentation; multiple case reports document melanoma emerging in users, although causality cannot be definitively established and confounding ultraviolet exposure is usually present.; Long-term safety, including
  *: PeptideDeck: Stimulates melanin production for skin tanning Increases sexual arousal and desire in both sexes May provide some UV protection through increased melanin Reduces appetite in some users Can induce tanning with minimal sun exposure Effects persist between dosing cycles Well-documented mechanism of action Melanotan II has been the subject of numerous clinical studies and research investigations, providing a substantial evidence base for its biological effects. This research has also informed the development of related compounds that have progressed to regulatory approval. Early human studies at the University of Arizona established that MT-2 could reliably induce skin darkening. In a foundational study, participants receiving MT-2 showed significant increases in skin melanin density as measured by reflectance spectroscopy. The tanning effect occurred even with limited UV exposure, though UV exposure enhanced and prolonged the response. A study published in Life Sciences (1996) examined MT-2's effects on human skin pigmentation and documented dose-dependent increases in tanning.
  *: PeptideDeck: Significant skin tanning with minimal sun exposure Protective melanin increase may reduce sunburn risk Notable increase in libido for both sexes Appetite suppression effects Tanning persists even without ongoing sun exposure More even tan without typical sun damage May help those who normally can't tan Effects develop over 1-2 weeks of use Active research area with published studies Active research area with published studies MT-II's research history is unusual-extensive early work on the mechanism, limited formal clinical development after safety signals emerged, and a large informal 'research' base of people using it cosmetically. The tanning effect is robust and well-documented. MT-II produces melanin. The sexual effects are equally well-documented, leading to PT-141 development. The appetite suppression is confirmed through melanocortin research. What's lacking: long-term safety data, proper dose-finding studies, and research on the cancer question-does MT-II protect against skin cancer (original theory) or potentially promote it (concern from mole changes)?
  *: Melanocortin receptor agonists, penile erection, and sexual motivation: human studies with Melanotan II (International Journal of Impotence Research 2000): Wessells et al. published the key human pharmacology study of Melanotan II, demonstrating dose-dependent penile erection and sexual motivation in men - the primary peer-reviewed human evidence for Melanotan II. Formal drug development subsequently pivoted to the derivative PT-141 (bremelanotide).

### compound | metenkephalin/overview | What is Met-Enkephalin?

title: Met-Enkephalin
summary: One of the body's endogenous opioid peptides (as Opioid Growth Factor, OGF), studied mainly through preclinical and mechanistic cancer-biology research. Human evidence includes early Phase I safety work and a small Phase II open-label study in advanced pancreatic cancer; neither establishes anticancer efficacy.

### compound | metenkephalin/evidence | What research is listed for Met-Enkephalin?
kind: evidence
title: Met-Enkephalin: research listed by the sources
summary: preliminary. Met-Enkephalin, also studied as Opioid Growth Factor (OGF), has reached early human oncology trials. Following Phase I investigation, a prospective Phase II open-label study treated 24 patients with advanced pancreatic cancer who had failed standard chemotherapy. Among participants surviving more than 8 weeks, 62% had either decreased or stable tumor size on imaging. Because the study was small, open-label, and relied partly on historical controls, these findings remain investigational and do not establish OGF as an effective pancreatic cancer treatment. The broader OGF-OGFr literature is largely preclinical and mechanistic, describing anti-proliferative effects of the OGF-OGFr axis in animal and cell-culture cancer models. This entry is included as an educational reference for the OGF-OGFr axis rather than as a practical or clinically supported research peptide; its 1-2 minute plasma half-life makes sustained exposure pharmacologically difficult without a depot formulation. Met-enkephalin is primarily used as a research tool in neuroscience and oncology studies. It is not currently approved as a therapeutic agent by any regulatory authority but has been investigated in clinical trials: Pancreatic Cancer: Phase II clinical trials of the OGF-OGFr axis as an adjunct to standard gemcitabine therapy for advanced pancreatic cancer Ovarian Cancer: Preclinical and early clinical investigation of OGF in combination with taxane-based chemotherapy Head and Neck Cancer: Investigation of OGF-OGFr pathway modulation in squamous cell carcinoma Autoimmune Conditions: Exploration of OGF's immunomodulatory properties in multiple sclerosis and other autoimmune disorders Reconstitution: Typically dissolved in sterile water, normal saline, or DMSO depending on experimental requirements Concentration: Stock solutions commonly prepared at 1-10 mM Storage: Reconstituted solutions should be aliquoted and stored at -20°C to -80°C Stability: Susceptible to oxidation of the methionine residue; avoid repeated freeze-thaw cycles [ 1 ] [ 2 ] [ 3 ] [ 4 ] [ 5 ] ↑ 1.0 1.1 Hughes J,

### compound | metformin/evidence | What research is listed for Metformin?
kind: evidence
title: Metformin: research listed by the sources
summary: FDA approved for T2D. Decades of human safety data. TAME longevity trial ongoing.
keyPoint: FDA approved for T2D.
understood: resolved
method: canonical
confidence: high
matchedText: Metformin
  connectedTo: Metformin
section: What the research shows
  -: The Peptide Handbook: An established prescription medicine for type 2 diabetes with separate, investigational aging research.
section: Evidence strength
  -: The Peptide Handbook: Randomized or controlled human research; population: Human; Direct controlled human evidence. The source does not give a reliable study count.
section: Limitations
  -: Lactic acidosis: rare but potentially fatal - risk is elevated with renal impairment, hepatic impairment, congestive heart failure, or excess alcohol use
  -: Contraindicated when eGFR is below 30 mL/min/1.73m²; use with caution when eGFR is 30-45 mL/min/1.73m²
  -: Vitamin B12 malabsorption: long-term use may reduce B12 absorption; periodic serum B12 monitoring is recommended per FDA labeling
  -: Iodinated contrast media: temporarily discontinue in patients with eGFR 30-60 mL/min/1.73m² before procedures using iodinated contrast; resume only after renal function is re-evaluated
  -: Drug interactions: cationic drugs (e.g., topiramate, cimetidine) may increase metformin plasma concentrations by competing for renal tubular secretion
  -: Prescription-only: should never be used without physician supervision, monitoring, and a documented clinical indication
  *: Source rating: 5 out of 5
  *: The Peptide Handbook: strong-human. The established evidence base for metformin is its use in type 2 diabetes. Bannister et al. reported retrospective mortality associations in people with type 2 diabetes; those observations cannot establish that metformin extends lifespan or benefit in healthy/non-diabetic people. Barzilai et al. provides scientific rationale for studying metformin in aging and the TAME concept, not completed TAME efficacy evidence. The completed MILES registry record describes a human randomized crossover Phase 4 study of biological effects in older adults with impaired glucose tolerance; a registry record is not proof of lifespan extension. Longevity and healthspan effects remain investigational and unproven.
  *: Metformin as a Tool to Target Aging (Cell Metabolism 2016): Rationale for TAME (Targeting Aging with Metformin) trial. Population data showing metformin users outlive matched non-diabetic controls.

### compound | methyleneblue/overview | What is Methylene Blue?
kind: overview
title: Methylene Blue
summary: Methylene Blue (methylthioninium chloride) is a synthetic phenothiazine dye and small-molecule mitochondrial/metabolic enhancer first synthesized in 1876, now used at low doses as a nootropic and at higher intravenous doses as an established antidote. It is a redox-active electron cycler: at low concentrations it accepts electrons from NADH and donates them to cytochrome c, bypassing complexes I-III to raise brain cytochrome c oxidase activity, cerebral oxygen consumption, and ATP output; at high concentrations it flips to a pro-oxidant, producing the classic hormetic, inverted-U dose-response. The most-studied Methylene Blue dosage for cognition is a single low oral dose of roughly 0.5-4 mg/kg (about 260-280 mg in controlled human fMRI and fear-extinction trials), while daily low-dose nootropic users typically take far less, on the order of 5-30 mg. It also potently inhibits monoamine oxidase-A and reduces methemoglobin back to functional hemoglobin.

### compound | methyleneblue/evidence | What research is listed for Methylene Blue?
kind: evidence
title: Methylene Blue: research listed by the sources
summary: Blue-green discoloration of urine, and sometimes stool, saliva, sweat, or sclera, is expected and harmless; the dye also stains skin, clothing, and surfaces on contact [6].; Serotonin syndrome is the most dangerous interaction: methylene blue is a potent reversible MAO-A inhibitor, and combining it with SSRIs, SNRIs, MAOIs, triptans, bupropion, buspirone, or other serotonergic agents has caused serious and even fatal reactions, prompting an FDA safety warning [7].; G6PD deficiency is a contraindication - at clinical doses methylene blue can precipitate severe hemolytic anemia in these individuals, so screening is advised before use, especially in people of African, Mediterranean, or South/Southeast Asian ancestry [6].; The dose-response is hormetic: above roughly 4 mg/kg the compound becomes a pro-oxidant, and high intravenous doses (≥7 mg/kg) can cause nausea, dyspnea, chest pain, tremor, confusion, hypertension, and paradoxical methemoglobinemia [6].; Lower-grade oral effects include gastrointestinal upset, mild bladder irritation or dysuria, headache, dizziness, and a transient

### compound | mgf/evidence | What research is listed for MGF?
kind: evidence
title: MGF: research listed by the sources
summary: Animal and in vitro data solid.
keyPoint: Animal and in vitro data solid.
understood: resolved
method: canonical
confidence: high
matchedText: MGF
  connectedTo: MGF
section: What the research shows
  -: The Peptide Handbook: MGF/IGF-1Ec is research terminology spanning endogenous expression biology, synthetic MGF-E peptides, and PEG-MGF; these are not interchangeable entities.
  -: Peptide Hub: MGF (Mechano Growth Factor) is an alternative splice variant of the IGF-1 gene, produced locally in skeletal muscle in response to mechanical stress and microtrauma such as resistance training.
  -: PeptideDosage.org: MGF (Mechano Growth Factor), more precisely IGF-1Ec, is a splice variant of the IGF-1 gene transcript that produces a precursor protein containing the mature IGF-1 sequence linked to a distinctive 24-amino-acid carboxy-terminal E-domain peptide.
  -: PeptideDeck: Recommended
  -: PeptideJournal: Mechano Growth Factor sounds like something from a superhero origin story.
section: Evidence strength
  -: The Peptide Handbook: Animal research; population: Animal; Preclinical animal evidence. The source does not give a reliable study count.
  -: Peptide Hub: Animal research; population: Animal; Preclinical animal evidence. The source does not give a reliable study count.
  -: PeptideDosage.org: Animal research; population: Animal; Preclinical animal evidence. The source does not give a reliable study count.
  -: PeptideDeck: Animal research; population: Animal; Preclinical animal evidence. The source does not give a reliable study count.
  -: PeptideJournal: Animal research; population: Animal; Preclinical animal evidence. The source does not give a reliable study count.
section: Limitations
  -: Long-term human safety data are not established.
  -: Research-material quality-control concerns may apply.
  -: This is a commercial educational source. Its uncited figures and modelled outputs must remain labelled as source-listed rather than clinical evidence.
  -: MGF (Mechano Growth Factor), more precisely IGF-1Ec, is a splice variant of the IGF-1 gene transcript that produces a precursor protein containing the mature IGF-1 sequence linked to a distinctive 24-amino-acid carboxy-terminal E-domain peptide.
  -: The reviewed record is animal research and cannot establish human effectiveness or safety.
  *: Source rating: 2 out of 5, limited evidence
  *: The Peptide Handbook: preliminary. The approved sources cover in-vitro human muscle-progenitor work, an animal myocardial-infarction experiment, and a review. They support an early-stage research framing only. Sport-status statements must be checked against the current WADA Prohibited List rather than inferred from preclinical evidence.
  *: Peptide Hub: Protocol-focused educational summary. Linked papers, site-listed ranges and commercial context are retained with source attribution.
  *: PeptideDosage.org: Localised injection-site pain and induration at the target muscle are the most commonly reported research-context adverse effect; the local concentration of peptide can produce acute discomfort lasting 2-6 hours.; Transient muscle pump and fullness within 30-60 minutes of local injection reflects acute satellite cell activation and fluid uptake; this is the desired pharmacodynamic signal but can be uncomfortable.; Theoretical concern for accelerated muscle-cell proliferation in the context of pre-existing rhabdomyosarcoma or other muscle-derived neoplasms; chronic use contraindicated in patients with muscle malignancy.; Sterile abscess or local infection at the injection site is reported with research-context use, often related to non-sterile reconstitution practice rather than the peptide itself.; Systemic effects are minimal because plasma half-life is 5-7 minutes; this is the key safety distinction from PEG-MGF and from systemic IGF-1 analogues.; No documented effect on glucose homeostasis from local MGF because the E-peptide does not engage the canonical IGF-1R/insulin receptor;
  *: PeptideDeck: Activates muscle satellite cells (muscle stem cells) Promotes local muscle repair following damage Supports muscle hypertrophy through hyperplasia May accelerate recovery from training Neuroprotective properties in research Local tissue-specific effects Complements systemic IGF-1 signaling May reduce muscle scarring after injury MGF research spans exercise physiology, muscle biology, and regenerative medicine, with consistent findings regarding its role in muscle adaptation and repair. Human studies have confirmed MGF expression increases in skeletal muscle following exercise, particularly following damaging eccentric contractions. A 2003 Journal of Physiology study showed MGF mRNA increased substantially in muscle biopsies taken after resistance exercise, with peak expression within hours of exercise and declining over 24-48 hours. This temporal pattern suggested MGF initiates the early repair response.
  *: PeptideJournal: Mechano Growth Factor sounds like something from a superhero origin story. In reality, it's a naturally occurring peptide your muscles produce every time you lift heavy, sprint hard, or push your body beyond its comfort zone. Mechano Growth Factor represents a fascinating piece of the muscle repair puzzle. Its rapid expression after mechanical stress, unique E domain structure, and ability to activate satellite cells without promoting their differentiation point to a specialized role as an injury response initiator. The breadth of effects seen in preclinical research-spanning muscle, nerve, bone, and cartilage-suggests MGF might be part of a general mechanotransduction system that helps tissues respond to physical stress. But interesting science doesn't equal proven therapy. MGF research remains almost entirely preclinical. No human clinical trials have tested whether it actually improves muscle growth, accelerates recovery, heals injuries, or provides any of the benefits its mechanism suggests it might.
  *: Different roles of the IGF-I Ec peptide (MGF) and mature IGF-I in myoblast proliferation and differentiation (FEBS Letters 2002): MGF E-peptide promotes myoblast proliferation and satellite cell activation independently of mature IGF-I, establishing the two-phase model of IGF-1 splice variant function in muscle repair.
  followUp: What does the research say about how MGF works?

  *: Resolved: site-listed dose ranges. Published study protocols with species, route, population, frequency and duration take priority. Uncited commercial ranges remain labelled and secondary. A product or calculator range is not evidence that a dose was studied, effective or safe. Confidence: high.
  *: Resolved: modelled administration routes. Use only the route stated in the original study or official product information. Do not convert an oral, intranasal, intramuscular or investigational product into a generic subcutaneous vial protocol. PeptideDosage.org applies a common reconstitution and syringe format even to products such as Ventfort that it identifies as oral. That format is not evidence that the modelled route was studied or is suitable. Confidence: high.
  *: Resolved: mental-health citation identity. Exclude three unrelated PubMed identifiers copied under Semax, NAC and Selank claims. Keep only links whose NCBI record matches the stated research subject. NCBI identifies PMID 11157505 as a Hodgkin-disease cell-fusion paper, PMID 16640009 as a Freeman-Sheldon syndrome case report, and PMID 18677858 as a neonatal-mortality paper. None supports the peptide claim beside which it appeared. Confidence: high.

  *: Source-listed components: SS-31, MOTS-c, NAD+.
  *: The approved terminology source gives a fixed component list. Product strengths and protocols can still vary.
  *: Terminology confidence: medium. Commercial source terminology only. Evidence for the three components is retrieved separately.
  *: Naming limitation: NAD+ product form and route vary by source.
  *: No source in the approved library establishes that the combination itself has the same evidence as its individual components.
  *: SS-31: Source rating: 3 out of 5. Clinical trials used 4mg and 40mg daily SubQ - but these were in SICK patients (heart failure, Barth syndrome). Healthy biohacker doses are far lower: 1-10 mg/day is the typical range. The 40mg TAZPOWER dose was for a rare genetic mitochondrial disease; it is not a biohacker target. Safety is well-established up to 40mg/day from trial data, but therapeutic need does not apply to healthy users. Doses shown above reflect biohacker practice, not clinical trial protocols.
  *: MOTS-c: Source rating: 2 out of 5, limited evidence. No completed human RCTs. Animal data strong. Human pilot studies range 5-10mg 2-3x weekly. Conservative approach recommended given experimental status. NOTE: Dosing protocols vary widely - some sources suggest daily low-dose (1-2mg), others suggest 5mg 2-3x weekly. We default to the more conservative 2-3x weekly protocol.
  *: NAD+: Source rating: 3 out of 5. Strong mechanistic data. Growing human IV NAD+ clinical trial base.

  *: No source in the approved library establishes that the combination itself has the same evidence as its individual components.
  *: SS-31: Source rating: 3 out of 5. Clinical trials used 4mg and 40mg daily SubQ - but these were in SICK patients (heart failure, Barth syndrome). Healthy biohacker doses are far lower: 1-10 mg/day is the typical range. The 40mg TAZPOWER dose was for a rare genetic mitochondrial disease; it is not a biohacker target. Safety is well-established up to 40mg/day from trial data, but therapeutic need does not apply to healthy users. Doses shown above reflect biohacker practice, not clinical trial protocols.
  *: MOTS-c: Source rating: 2 out of 5, limited evidence. No completed human RCTs. Animal data strong. Human pilot studies range 5-10mg 2-3x weekly. Conservative approach recommended given experimental status. NOTE: Dosing protocols vary widely - some sources suggest daily low-dose (1-2mg), others suggest 5mg 2-3x weekly. We default to the more conservative 2-3x weekly protocol.
  *: NAD+: Source rating: 3 out of 5. Strong mechanistic data. Growing human IV NAD+ clinical trial base.
